decks.title: Reflection of Light at Plane Mirrors — Part 1: Laws of reflection and the image
goals: State the laws of reflection and describe the pin experiment that verifies them
Calculate angles of incidence and reflection and locate the image of a point object
List the characteristics of the image in a plane mirror, explain lateral inversion and give uses of plane mirrors

slides.heading: How does a mirror turn light around?
slides.body_md: Part 1 — light bounces off a mirror by a simple rule that we can test.

visual.alt: Flow from a light ray striking a mirror to the ray bouncing back by a rule

slides.narration: Look at yourself in a mirror and you see a face that seems to sit behind the glass. This part shows the simple rule that decides where every ray of light goes after it hits a mirror.

slides.heading: Words we need
slides.body_md: A ray falling on a mirror is the **incident ray**; the ray that leaves is the **reflected ray**. The **normal** is the line at **90°** to the mirror at the **point of incidence**. The **angle of incidence** ($i$) and the **angle of reflection** ($r$) are measured **from the normal**, not from the mirror.

rows: Ray that falls on the mirror
Ray that bounces off the mirror
Perpendicular to the mirror at the point of incidence
Between the incident ray and the normal
Between the reflected ray and the normal

visual.alt: Table of the terms used in reflection and their meanings

slides.narration: The normal is a line standing straight up from the mirror at the point where the ray lands. Both angles are measured from this line. Many students wrongly measure from the mirror surface, so be careful.

slides.heading: The two laws of reflection
slides.body_md: **First law:** the angle of incidence is **equal to** the angle of reflection, $i = r$. **Second law:** the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the **same plane**. A ray along the normal has $i = 0$ and returns along its own path.

slides.narration: Two pins mark the incident ray. Looking in the mirror, you place two more pins so that they line up with the images of the first two. The line through the last pins is the reflected ray, and a protractor measures both angles.

slides.heading: What the readings show
slides.body_md: Repeat for different incident rays. Within the error of measurement, **i = r** every time, and the reflected ray lies in the plane of the paper. Small differences of 1 or 1° come from reading the protractor.

visual.alt: Table of sample readings of the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection

slides.narration: The measured angles of reflection agree with the angles of incidence to within one degree. The small differences come from reading the protractor, not from the law, which holds exactly.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: angles at a mirror
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A ray strikes a plane mirror so that it makes 40° with the mirror surface. Find the angle of incidence, the angle of reflection and the angle between the incident and reflected rays.

**Step 1.** Angle of incidence $= 90° - 40° = 50°$.

**Step 2.** By the first law, $r = 50°$, so the angle between the rays $= 50° + 50° = 100°$.

visual.alt: Table of the working for the angle of incidence, the angle of reflection and the angle between the rays

slides.narration: The ray makes forty degrees with the mirror, so it makes fifty degrees with the normal. The reflected ray also makes fifty with the normal, so the angle between the incident and reflected rays is one hundred degrees.

slides.heading: The image of a point in a plane mirror
slides.body_md: Rays from a point object O reflect as if they came from a point **I behind the mirror**. Trace the reflected rays **backwards** (dotted) and they meet at I. The line OI is **perpendicular** to the mirror, and **IM = OM**: the image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

slides.heading: Characteristics of the image
slides.body_md: The image in a plane mirror is **virtual** (it cannot be caught on a screen), **erect**, **the same size** as the object, **as far behind the mirror as the object is in front**, and **laterally inverted**.

rows: Equal to the distance of the object from the mirror

visual.alt: Table of the five characteristics of the image in a plane mirror

slides.narration: The image seems to sit behind the mirror but no light really reaches it, so it is virtual and cannot appear on a screen. It is upright, the same size, as far behind as the object is in front, and turned left to right.

slides.heading: Lateral inversion
slides.body_md: In a plane mirror the **left side of the object appears as the right side of the image**. A letter like F looks reversed. This is **lateral inversion**. The word AMBULANCE is printed reversed on the front of the vehicle so that a driver sees it correctly in the rear-view mirror.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: distances to the image
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A candle is 24 cm in front of a plane mirror. Find the distance of the image from the mirror and the distance between the candle and its image.

**Step 1.** The image is as far behind as the object is in front: $v = 24$ cm.

**Step 2.** Distance between object and image $= 24 + 24 = 48$ cm.

visual.alt: Table of the working for the image distance and the distance between the object and its image

slides.narration: The image is twenty-four centimetres behind the mirror. The distance from the candle to its image adds the two equal distances, which is forty-eight centimetres.

slides.heading: Uses of plane mirrors
slides.body_md: Plane mirrors are used in **dressing tables and shops**, in **periscopes** (two mirrors at **45°** let us see over a wall or from a submarine), in **kaleidoscopes** (mirrors at an angle make patterns), in **barbers’ shops** (to view the back of the head) and in **instrument scales** to avoid reading errors.

slides.body_md: Part 2 — an image can itself act as an object for the other mirror.

visual.alt: Flow from an object to its image in the first mirror and then to that image acting as an object for the second mirror

slides.narration: In a barber’s shop you may see a long line of images when two mirrors face each other. The reason is simple: the image formed by one mirror becomes the object for the other mirror.

slides.heading: Two parallel plane mirrors
slides.body_md: Place an object O between two parallel mirrors M1 and M2. M1 makes the image **I1** and M2 makes **I2**. Then **I1 acts as an object for M2** and **I2 for M1**, giving **I3** and **I4**, and so on. In principle the number of images is **infinite**. In the figure the mirrors are 40 cm apart and O is 10 cm from M1.

slides.narration: The first mirror forms one image and the second mirror forms another. Each of those images is then reflected again by the opposite mirror. The process never ends, so the images are very many and line up in rows behind each mirror.

slides.heading: Finding the positions by reflection
slides.body_md: To locate each image, reflect the previous image in the next mirror, which is the same distance **behind** the mirror as the image is in front. With O at 10 cm from M1 and the mirrors 40 cm apart, the first images are 10 cm behind M1 (I1) and 30 cm behind M2 (I2). I3 is the image of I2 in M1, and I4 is the image of I1 in M2.

visual.alt: Table of the first four images in two parallel mirrors and their distances behind the mirrors

slides.narration: Each new image is found by reflecting the one before it in the other mirror. The distances behind the mirrors increase each time, so the images spread out in a line on each side.

slides.heading: Why the images become fainter
slides.body_md: At each reflection a small part of the light is **absorbed** by the mirror and part passes through or is scattered, so **less light reaches the eye** from each later image. The **successive images become fainter** and the far ones cannot be seen.

visual.alt: Table of how the brightness of the images falls with the number of reflections

slides.narration: No mirror reflects all the light that falls on it. At every reflection some light is lost. An image that has been reflected many times is therefore fainter than one reflected only once.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: distances in parallel mirrors
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** An object is 10 cm from mirror M1 and 30 cm from mirror M2 (40 cm apart). Find the distance between the object and the first image formed by M2.

**Step 1.** First image in M2 is 30 cm behind M2.

**Step 2.** Distance from O $= 30 + 30 = 60$ cm.

rows: Equal to the object distance from M2

visual.alt: Table of the working for the distance between the object and the first image in M2

slides.narration: The object is thirty centimetres from the second mirror, so its image is thirty centimetres behind that mirror. The distance between the object and this image is therefore sixty centimetres.

slides.heading: Two mirrors at an angle
slides.body_md: When two mirrors meet at an **angle θ**, the object and all its images lie on a **circle** whose centre is where the mirrors meet. The images are found by repeated reflection. At **90°** three images are formed: **I1** in M1, **I2** in M2, and **I3**, the image of I1 in M2 (or of I2 in M1), formed by **two** reflections.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting images

**Problem.** Two plane mirrors are inclined at 60°. How many images are formed? What if they are at 72° and the object is (i) on the bisector, (ii) not on it?

notes.title: Reflection of Light at Plane Mirrors — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Laws of reflection and their verification
sections.body_md:
**Terms.** The ray that falls on the mirror is the **incident ray**; the ray sent back is the **reflected ray**. The **normal** is the perpendicular to the mirror at the **point of incidence**. The **angle of incidence** $i$ and the **angle of reflection** $r$ are measured **from the normal**.

**Laws of reflection**
1. The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection: $i = r$.
2. The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the **same plane**.

A ray along the normal has $i = 0$ and is reflected back along its own path. If a ray makes an angle $\alpha$ with the mirror, then $i = 90° - \alpha$.

**Verification (pin experiment).** On a sheet of paper draw a line for the mirror and a normal ON at O. Fix pins **P1 and P2** on a line through O (the incident ray). Looking into the mirror, fix **P3 and P4** so that they appear in line with the **images** of P1 and P2. Remove the mirror and pins, join P3P4 to O, and measure $\angle i$ and $\angle r$ with a protractor. Repeat for other angles. Within experimental error $i = r$, and the pins lie flat on the paper, which shows the second law. **Precautions:** keep the pins vertical; fix P3 and P4 by looking at the bases of the images; keep the mirror edge on the line.

sections.heading: 3. Images in two mirrors
sections.body_md:
**Parallel mirrors.** An image formed in one mirror acts as an **object** for the other, so an object between two parallel mirrors forms **many** images (infinite in principle). Locate them by repeated reflection. With O 10 cm from M1 and the mirrors 40 cm apart, I1 is 10 cm behind M1, I2 is 30 cm behind M2, I3 (image of I2 in M1) is 70 cm behind M1, I4 (image of I1 in M2) is 50 cm behind M2. **Brightness:** some light is lost (absorbed, scattered) at each reflection, so **successive images are fainter**.

**Inclined mirrors.** For mirrors at angle $\theta$ the object and its images lie on a circle centred at the meeting point of the mirrors. If $\dfrac{360}{\theta}$ is a whole number:
- **even** $\dfrac{360}{\theta}$: $n = \dfrac{360}{\theta} - 1$ for any position of the object;
- **odd** $\dfrac{360}{\theta}$: $n = \dfrac{360}{\theta} - 1$ if the object is on the **bisector**, otherwise $n = \dfrac{360}{\theta}$.

Examples: 90° gives 3; 60° gives 5; 45° gives 7; 30° gives 11. As $\theta$ tends to 0 the mirrors become parallel and the number of images becomes infinite. Textbooks differ on the odd case; this chapter uses the rule above, which can be checked by drawing the images.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Measuring the angle of incidence from the mirror instead of from the normal.
- Drawing the reflected rays behind the mirror with continuous lines instead of dotted lines.
- Calling the image in a plane mirror real, or forgetting lateral inversion.
- Forgetting the "− 1" in n = 360 ÷ θ − 1, or ignoring the odd case.
- Saying that far images are fainter because they are farther away (the reason is the loss of light at each reflection).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Laws (2 marks): both laws, with "i = r" and "in the same plane".
- Diagrams (2 to 3 marks): normal dotted, arrows on rays, dotted lines behind the mirror, labels.
- Numericals (1 to 3 marks): angle from the normal, distances, number of images with the formula shown.

questions.stem_md:
A student verifies a law of reflection with pins and a plane mirror. For four different incident rays she measures the angle of incidence i and the angle of reflection r from the normal.

| i (degrees) | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| r (degrees) | 20 | 31 | 40 | 49 |

(a) State the law of reflection that she is verifying. [1]

(b) Describe how she marks the incident ray and the reflected ray. [3]

(c) Find the mean value of i and the mean value of r, and state the conclusion. [3]

(d) Give one reason why the readings of i and r differ slightly. [1]

(e) State two precautions she should take. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The **angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection**.

**(b)** She fixes pins **P1 and P2** along the incident ray. Looking into the mirror, she fixes pins **P3 and P4** so that they appear **in line with the images** of P1 and P2; the line through P3 and P4 is the reflected ray.

**(c)** Mean $i = \dfrac{20 + 30 + 40 + 50}{4} = 35°$; mean $r = \dfrac{20 + 31 + 40 + 49}{4} = 35°$. They are **equal**, which verifies that $i = r$.

**(d)** The angles are read with a protractor, so there is a **small error of reading**.

**(e)** Keep the **pins vertical**; fix P3 and P4 by looking at the **bases** of the images; keep the mirror exactly on its line (any two).

questions.solution_md: i equals r; P1 P2 incident, P3 P4 aligned with images; both means 35°, equal; reading error; pins vertical and sight bases.

marking_scheme.step: P1 and P2 on the incident ray
P3 and P4 in line with the images
Reflected ray joined through P3 and P4

questions.stem_md:
A boy stands 2 m in front of a large plane mirror.

(a) Find the distance between the boy and his image. [1]

(b) He walks 0.5 m towards the mirror. Find the new distance between him and his image. [2]

(c) He walks towards the mirror at 1.5 m s⁻¹. Find the speed at which his image approaches him. [2]

(d) State three characteristics of the image. [3]

(e) He holds a card showing the letter P up to the mirror. Describe what he sees in the mirror, and name the effect. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The image is 2 m behind the mirror, so the distance $= 2 + 2 = 4$ m.

**(b)** His distance from the mirror $= 2 - 0.5 = 1.5$ m, so the distance between him and the image $= 2 \times 1.5 = 3$ m.

**(c)** The image also moves at 1.5 m s⁻¹ towards the mirror, so it approaches him at $1.5 + 1.5 = 3$ m s⁻¹.

**(d)** Any three: **virtual**, **erect**, **same size**, **as far behind the mirror as the object is in front**, **laterally inverted**.

**(e)** He sees the letter P **turned left to right** (reversed); this is **lateral inversion**.

questions.solution_md: 4 m; 3 m; 3 m s⁻¹; virtual, erect, same size; reversed P, lateral inversion.

marking_scheme.step: Letter appears reversed left to right

questions.stem_md:
The figure shows an object O between two parallel plane mirrors M1 and M2, which are 40 cm apart. O is 10 cm from M1.

(a) Find the distance of the first image formed by M1 from M1, and the distance of the first image formed by M2 from M2. [2]

(b) Find the distance between these two first images. [2]

(c) The first image formed by M1 acts as an object for M2. Find the distance of the image it forms from M2. [2]

(d) Why do the later images become fainter? [2]

(e) State the number of images formed in principle and give a reason. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Behind M1: **10 cm**; behind M2: $40 - 10 = $ **30 cm**.

**(b)** Taking M1 as zero, the first image in M1 is at -10 cm and the first image in M2 is at 70 cm along the line, so the distance between them $= 70 + 10 = 80$ cm.

**(c)** The first image in M1 is 50 cm from M2, so the new image is **50 cm** behind M2.

**(d)** A part of the light is **absorbed or lost at each reflection**, so each later image is less bright.

**(e)** **Infinite**, because the image formed in one mirror always acts as an object for the other mirror.

questions.solution_md: 10 cm and 30 cm; 80 cm; 50 cm; light is lost at each reflection; infinite, each image is an object for the other mirror.

marking_scheme.step: So later images are less bright
Each image acts as an object for the other mirror

questions.stem_md:
The figure shows two plane mirrors M1 and M2 at right angles to each other, with an object O between them. Three images, lettered P, Q and R, are formed.

(a) State the number of images formed when two plane mirrors are inclined at an angle θ, in terms of θ. [1]

(b) Which of the images P, Q and R is formed by two reflections? [1]

(c) Find the number of images when the mirrors are inclined at (i) 60° and (ii) 45°. [3]

(d) The mirrors are now inclined at 72°. Find the number of images when the object is (i) on the bisector and (ii) not on the bisector. [3]

(e) What happens to the number of images as the mirrors are brought nearer to parallel? [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $n = \dfrac{360}{\theta} - 1$ (when $\dfrac{360}{\theta}$ is a whole number).

**(b)** Image **Q**, which is the image of the image formed in the other mirror.

**(c)** **(i)** $\dfrac{360}{60} - 1 = 5$. **(ii)** $\dfrac{360}{45} - 1 = 7$.

**(d)** $\dfrac{360}{72} = 5$ is odd. **(i)** On the bisector: $5 - 1 = 4$. **(ii)** Off the bisector: 5.

**(e)** The number of images **increases**, and becomes **infinite** when the mirrors are parallel.

questions.solution_md: n = 360/θ − 1; the double-reflection image; 5 and 7; 4 and 5; increases without limit.

questions.stem_md:
The figure shows the ray of light through a periscope, with its parts lettered A to E. A is the top mirror and B is the bottom mirror.

(a) Name the parts C, D and E. [3]

(b) State the angle that each mirror makes with the axis of the tube and the angle of incidence of the ray on each mirror. [3]

(c) State two characteristics of the final image seen by the observer. [2]

(d) Two plane mirrors inclined at 60° are used in a kaleidoscope. Find the number of images formed of a bead placed between them. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **C** is the ray from the object (incident on the top mirror); **D** is the ray travelling down the tube; **E** is the ray reaching the eye.

**(b)** Each mirror makes an angle of **45°** with the axis of the tube. The ray falls on each mirror at an angle of incidence of **45°**, so it is turned through **90°** by each mirror.

**(c)** The image is **virtual**, **erect** and of the **same size** as the object (any two).

**(d)** $n = \dfrac{360}{60} - 1 = 5$ images.

questions.solution_md: Incident ray, ray in the tube, ray to the eye; 45° and 45°; virtual and erect; 5 images.
